content:
You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Final answer format. First list the passages you rely on, copied VERBATIM from the files (no
  paraphrase, no ellipsis inside the quotation marks), then write the answer using only them:
  <evidence>
  [E1] "exact text" (file)
  [E2] "exact text" (file)
  </evidence>
  <answer>
  Your answer to the user. End every factual sentence with the evidence it rests on, e.g. [E1] or
  [E1, E2]. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no marker.
  </answer>
- The user sees only the <answer> part, so it must be complete and readable on its own.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Can you summarize the following text in bullet form. Each bullet must contain a quote from the passage supporting the summary point but still describe the points. Don't use the word AI and make sure to talk about all of the points made. PLease provide some specific examples and names/descriptions of organizations and can you describe the code of conduct stuff? Talk about specific acts and list out specific guidelines they are implementing. Limit it to 400 words.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	Abraham Lincoln once observed: “In the world’s history, certain inventions and discoveries occurred
     2	of peculiar value . . . in facilitating all other inventions and discoveries.” Lincoln was speaking
     3	of the written word and, later, the printing press. But today, we are living through another such
     4	invention: artificial intelligence.
     5	
     6	
     7	 Powerful generative AI systems like GPT-4 are ushering in a new era of this technology. They’re
     8	revolutionising the production of knowledge: vastly increasing the capacity of machines to generate
     9	original content, perform complex tasks and solve important problems. They are also dramatically
    10	lowering the barriers for people to access AI and its benefits.
    11	
    12	
    13	 This new era brings serious potential hazards. These include the risk of AI generating false
    14	information, reinforcing bias and discrimination, being misused for repressive or destabilising
    15	purposes or proliferating the knowledge to make a bioweapon or conduct a cyber attack.
    16	
    17	
    18	 But even with these risks — which we’re determined to minimise — AI holds an exhilarating potential
    19	to improve people’s lives and help solve some of the world’s biggest challenges, from curing cancer
    20	to mitigating the effects of climate change to solving global food insecurity.
    21	
    22	
    23	 The future of AI — whether it makes our societies more or less equitable, unlocks breakthroughs or
    24	becomes a tool of authoritarians — is up to us. The question is not whether to use it, but how.
    25	
    26	
    27	 The United States, as home to many of the leading companies, technologies and minds driving the AI
    28	revolution, has the ability and responsibility to lead on its governance. We are committed to doing
    29	so in partnership with others around the world to ensure the future reflects our shared values and
    30	vision for this technology.
    31	
    32	
    33	 We have already taken action to guide AI’s use. We set out a Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights
    34	with principles for how automated systems are designed and used, and developed an AI Risk Management
    35	Framework to help improve user protections.
    36	
    37	
    38	 Last week, President Joe Biden announced the next step with a set of commitments from leading
    39	companies designed to enhance safety, security and trust. These commitments will mitigate risks of
    40	AI including misuse, and support new technologies and standards to distinguish between human and
    41	AI-generated content. They will encourage companies and individuals to report on systems’
    42	capabilities and limitations, and facilitate information sharing. And they will promote the
    43	development of AI systems designed to address society’s greatest challenges.
    44	
    45	
    46	 The commitments offer a starting point for action to limit near-term risks while fostering
    47	innovation. They will be complemented by key lines of effort with partners around the world.
    48	
    49	
    50	 Over the coming weeks, we will continue to work with the G7 through the Japan-led Hiroshima Process
    51	to expand and internationalise these commitments. We want AI governance to be guided by democratic
    52	values and those who embrace them, and G7-led action could inform an international code of conduct
    53	for private actors and governments, as well as common regulatory principles for states. As we
    54	co-ordinate globally, we will also align our domestic approaches in forums like the US-EU Trade and
    55	Technology Council.
    56	
    57	
    58	 We will work intensively with other governments to build a shared understanding of longer-term AI
    59	risks and how to limit them. The US looks forward to participating in the UK’s Global Summit on AI
    60	Safety and other opportunities for global engagement to build a more secure future.
    61	
    62	
    63	 The US is committed to making AI work for, and designing governance with, developing countries,
    64	whose voices are crucial to the global discussion. India will play a critical role, including
    65	through the Global Partnership on AI. We are also working on inclusivity for AI through discussions
    66	with the UN.
    67	
    68	
    69	 We will partner with countries around the world, as well as the private sector and civil society,
    70	to advance a key goal of the commitments: creating AI systems that make people’s lives better.
    71	Today, we’re on track to meet just 12 per cent of the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals. AI could
    72	change that trajectory by accelerating efforts to deliver clean water and sanitation, eliminate
    73	poverty, advance public health and further other development goals.
    74	
    75	
    76	 To shape the future of AI, we must act quickly. We must also act collectively. No country or
    77	company can shape the future of AI alone. The US has taken an important step — but only with the
    78	combined focus, ingenuity and co-operation of the international community will we be able to fully
    79	and safely harness the potential of AI.
    80	
    81	
    82	 The writers are US secretary of state and US secretary of commerce
